narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.79). This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor. At 38, your score sits slightly above the average of accepted students (37.18), which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class standing.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Placing in the third decile (well below the accepted-student average of 6.0) added further weight toward a failure prediction.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently lower class rankings as the dominant signal, outweighing your solid LSAT result. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class rank in future semesters, or consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (248 words)
